## The question

I still start with the measure. I ask an assistant to write the calculation, and a formula comes back before anyone has said what the number is allowed to mean. The report runs. The meeting treats the result as specified, when all that happened is that a formula executed.

[Understanding DAX contracts when using AI](https://www.sqlbi.com/tv/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) is Alberto Ferrari's note from this week. I did not watch the video. I read the [article](https://www.sqlbi.com/articles/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) he and Marco Russo published beside it on 5 October 2026. Their worked example ranks customers in DAX, the formula language in Power BI, Microsoft's reporting product. Under that example, the page that states how a model is allowed to compute is the thing to review.

They call that page a contract. The formula is what the assistant writes once the page exists. The semantic model, the layer under the report where the measures live, should follow the page. A colleague should be able to argue with those sentences and never open the model.

## The rule was already missing

I know this failure from reports I have had to inherit. Someone could state the business rule in the meeting. The write-up went unread. Months later the only accurate description was a measure one person could still parse. Russo and Ferrari describe that same habit across years of business intelligence. Self-service BI, where the person who knew the business also built the model, left the rule inside the formula anyway. I treat the history as their account. It matches the files I have opened.

An assistant shortens the path from request to formula, so the missing page is easier to skip. People skip documentation. An assistant will draft the rules and rewrite the formula after the page changes. The page was the chore I postponed, and now it is the edit I make first.

## Settle the page, then ask for the formula

They ask which questions have to be settled, save the answers, read the wording the assistant stored, patch what is still open, and only then request the formula. In the article that formula ranks customers, and it runs long. The page is short enough to hand to someone who will never read DAX. It says which filters change the number, and what a total means when the row is more than one thing. When the rule changes, they change the page and ask for a new formula.

They show that formula on a matrix I have not reproduced, and they leave the production check outside the article. The order is what I can reuse the next time a team has to defend a number.

**I change the page before I change the formula.**

## A clear page can still be the wrong rule

They close by saying that, to their knowledge so far, a contract has no drawbacks. A clear page can describe the wrong business rule, and the assistant will follow it. While I am still searching for the question, I mark the page as a sketch, so a trial does not quietly become the rule.

I have not done the read-back on a model I maintain. The assistant stores its own wording, and they tell you to compare it with what you typed. Until I do that, I will not call the cleanup safe.

Monday is one calculation. The first message asks what has to be settled. I save the answer beside the model and read the stored version before I ask for code. Then I explain one result out loud from the page alone. If I need the formula to finish the sentence, the page is unfinished, and the measure stays out of any report the team will treat as settled.

## Takeaway

I keep a short page that says how the number is allowed to behave, and I change that page before I change the formula. If I cannot explain one result from the page alone, the formula does not ship.
